summary: For ages 9–10, children apply scientific ideas to design, build, [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-4] a starting source into a useful output (e.g. battery+buzzer for sound, battery+bulb for light, battery+motor car for motion, wound-elastic racer, black-cup passive solar heater, simple windmill). The science stays qualitative — name the input (e.g. a battery, wound elastic, sunlight or moving air) and the useful output — and the heart of the task is the design→test→refine cycle under real constraints (materials, time), not efficiency formulas. The honest framing is that a device TRANSFERS energy from a starting store or carrier to a useful output (some always spreads to the surroundings); it never creates energy. A hands-on build kit is the authentic home for this objective; a screen design-bench is a companion for rehearsing the energy-flow reasoning and the iteration loop, and a cutaway reference or matching/sequence task supports naming and consolidation.
misconceptions: 'The device makes/produces energy' from nothing — it converts a starting store (battery, sunlight, wound spring); name the input every time to break the free-energy idea.
'Energy changes form' taken literally as a substance morphing — reframe as energy TRANSFERRED from one store/carrier to another, so KS3 store-and-pathway teaching isn't undermined.
Expecting 100% of the input to become the useful output — some always spreads to the surroundings (warmth, wasted light/sound); kept qualitative here.
Treating the FIRST build as the finished answer — missing that test-and-refine (iteration) is the point of the task.
Confusing 'it works' with 'it meets the goal/constraints' — a device can run but still fail the brief (too slow, uses too much, wrong output).

activities.title: Design, build and refine a real energy-converting device
steps: Take a design brief with a measurable-enough goal, e.g. 'make the buggy cross this line', 'warm the water in the cup', or 'make the buzzer sound'.

Choose an energy source and a matching converter from real kit: a battery with a motor, bulb or buzzer; a wound elastic band turning an axle and wheels; sunlight on a black cup (or foil reflector); or moving air turning windmill blades; plus parts (wheels, card, black cup, foil).
Build a first version, then TEST it against the goal and record what actually happened (did it cross the line? how far? how warm?).
State the energy story out loud: name where the energy starts and the useful output, e.g. 'stored chemical energy in the battery → the motor turns → the wheels move'.
Identify ONE specific weakness from the test evidence, change just that one thing (fresher/bigger source, lighter load), and re-test to see if it improved.

Point to the part where the energy is transferred to the useful output (e.g. the motor, where the electric current makes it spin), and name any energy that spread to the surroundings (e.g. the motor got warm, or some light or sound was wasted).
activities.insight: A device moves energy from a starting source to a useful output — it never makes energy from nothing — and the first build is meant to be improved: targeted test-and-refine, not random tinkering, is the point of the task.

activities.title: On-screen design-bench to rehearse the energy flow and the refine loop
steps: Pick an energy source from a palette (battery, wound elastic, or a sunbeam) and snap it to a converter and load that can use it (e.g. battery to motor, bulb or buzzer; wound elastic to an axle and wheels; sunbeam to a black cup of water); a pairing that cannot work, such as a sunbeam straight to a motor with no solar cell, should not run.
Take a goal card (e.g. 'make the car cross the line' / 'warm the water') and run the test.
Watch the input→output energy-flow strip light up (e.g. battery [chemical] → motor → wheels [motion]) and note the small 'to surroundings' leak as the motor warms.
When the buggy crawls halfway and stops, use a refine panel to change ONE thing — swap to a bigger source or a lighter load — and re-test, with each attempt logged so the iteration is visible.
Try building a device with NO energy source and see the bench refuse to run ('where is the energy coming from?').
activities.insight: The device only ever moves energy from a starting source to a useful output, the first try is meant to be improved, and a device with no energy source cannot do anything — there is no free energy.

activities.title: Cutaway reference: name the input→output story of real devices
steps: Explore a tappable cutaway of real devices (torch, buzzer car, solar heater).
For each, read out its energy story, e.g. tap a torch → 'chemical (battery) → electrical → light'.
Compare devices and say which starting source and which useful output each uses.
activities.insight: Every device has a nameable energy story: a starting source feeding through a converter to a useful output.

activities.title: Consolidation: match devices to conversions and order the design loop
steps: Match each device to its input→output conversion (device → conversion).
Put the steps of the design loop in order: design → build → test → refine.
Answer 'where does the energy come from?' style questions, choosing the starting source.
activities.insight: Secure recall that devices convert from a named source, and that engineering follows a repeating design→build→test→refine loop.

checkQuestion: Using these materials — a small motor, a battery and wires, card, elastic bands, a buzzer and a bulb — design and build a device that turns one form of energy into another (for example electrical energy into movement, or movement into sound). Build it, test whether it works, then change one thing to make it work better. As you go, tell me what form of energy is turning into what. I'll watch rather than help.
checkAnswer: The child builds a working device (e.g. battery → motor spinning a card fan: chemical → electrical → kinetic; or a plucked elastic band across a box: kinetic → sound), tests it, identifies a specific weakness, makes one purposeful change that improves it, and correctly names the energy conversion at each stage — including energy that ends up as unwanted heat or sound.
